Indigestion is a noun that refers to the physical discomfort or pain you feel in your stomach — and sometimes in your chest — when your body is struggling to break down the food you have eaten properly. It is not a disease in itself, but rather a symptom or a collection of unpleasant feelings that tells you something is not going smoothly with your digestive process.

Think of your stomach as a machine whose job is to process food. Indigestion is what happens when that machine has trouble doing its job — the food sits there, causes pressure, and makes you feel awful.

Indigestion is not a single, sharp feeling. It is more of a cluster of uncomfortable sensations, which is why the word covers a range of experiences:

A feeling of being uncomfortably full, even after eating only a little. A burning or gnawing sensation in the upper part of your stomach or behind your breastbone. Bloating, where your stomach feels swollen and tight like a balloon. You might also feel nauseous, burp a lot, or feel an unpleasant acidic taste rising up into your throat. None of these are pleasant, and together they make up what we call indigestion.

Indigestion can be triggered by many things. Eating too fast, eating too much, or eating rich, greasy, or very spicy food are the most common causes. Drinking too much coffee or alcohol, smoking, stress and anxiety, and even certain medicines can also bring it on. In some cases, it is caused by a deeper medical condition like acid reflux or a stomach ulcer, but very often it is simply the result of something harmless you ate or how you ate it.

Indigestion is used in everyday conversation as well as in medical contexts. It is a countable and uncountable noun, meaning you can say both "I have indigestion" (uncountable, referring to the condition in general) and "I had a terrible bout of indigestion last night" (using it with a describing phrase). You will rarely say "an indigestion" on its own.

Here are some natural examples of the word in use:

  • "I think the pizza gave me indigestion."
  • "She has been suffering from indigestion for weeks and finally went to see a doctor."
  • "Eating right before bed is a common cause of indigestion."
  • "He reached for some antacid tablets to relieve his indigestion."
  • "Stress can sometimes trigger indigestion even when you have eaten perfectly well."
The Medical Side of the Word

In formal medical language, indigestion is also called dyspepsia. You may encounter this word in a doctor's office or in clinical writing. The two words mean the same thing, but "indigestion" is the everyday, plain-English version that most people use in normal conversation, while "dyspepsia" is the clinical term used by doctors.

Since you want a complete picture, it helps to know the family of words this noun belongs to:

The verb is digest, meaning the process of breaking food down in your body. "Your stomach digests food." The noun form of that process is digestion, meaning the overall system or act of digesting. "Good digestion is important for health." When something is hard for your body to process, you call it indigestible (adjective) — "Heavy fried food can be indigestible." And digestive is the adjective used to describe things related to the digestion system — "digestive enzymes," "the digestive tract."

So, indigestion literally means the failure or difficulty of digestion — the prefix "in-" signals the absence or reversal of something, the way "invisible" means not visible or "incomplete" means not complete.

There are several words and phrases that overlap with indigestion, and knowing them will sharpen your understanding:

Heartburn is closely related but more specific — it refers to the burning sensation in the chest caused by stomach acid rising up. It is one of the things that can happen during indigestion, but not the only one. People sometimes use heartburn and indigestion interchangeably in casual speech, though they are not technically identical.

Upset stomach is a loose, informal phrase that can mean indigestion or simply any stomach discomfort. It is vaguer and more conversational.

Acid reflux refers specifically to stomach acid flowing backwards up into the oesophagus (the tube connecting your mouth and stomach), and it is one of the common causes of indigestion.

Nausea means the feeling of wanting to vomit, which can accompany indigestion but is not the same thing.

Occasionally, though not very commonly, "indigestion" is used figuratively to describe the feeling of being overwhelmed by too much of something — particularly too much information or too many new ideas at once. For example: "The students suffered from intellectual indigestion after three lectures in a row." This is a metaphor comparing an overloaded mind to an overloaded stomach, and while it is not a dominant usage, you may encounter it in essays or literary writing. In everyday speech, stick to the physical meaning.

In short, indigestion (noun) means the discomfort and pain caused by difficulty in digesting food. It describes what happens in your stomach and chest when your digestive system is not working smoothly — whether because of what you ate, how much you ate, your stress levels, or an underlying condition. It is a very common, everyday word used by ordinary people and doctors alike, and it belongs to a family of words built around the central idea of breaking down food in the body.
